$about: 2026-08-06, shape round: the nine open findings in the shape area re-run against the current tree before anything was changed, then fixed where the fix was the standard's to make. All nine still reproduced. Seven are closed here and two are left open on purpose - each of those has a half that is a decision for the maintainer rather than an author's guess, and the waiver states the options. Every fix in this round is rule-text or catalogue text except one, which is code and carries tests.

$elicitation.$why: This corpus measures whether the tooling conforms - gates, manifests, drift counts. No person was prompted in any of these runs and none was meant to be, so it evidences nothing about whether the standard asks anybody anything. It was never labelled that way, which is how 377 green observations came to read as validation of a product whose central promise is being guided.

observations.evidence: Reproduced first, by the case's own procedure: the integration rule opened `The mainline's history MUST read as one finished unit of work per PR`, and continued `Every PR MUST be based on the mainline, never on another open PR's branch` and `A PR MUST land by rebase-merge (the paved road) or squash-merge`. Every clause named the pull request, and `grep -rni` for 'mailing list', 'patch series' and 'gerrit' across the whole checkout returned two hits, both inside ADR-026's prose about merge queues, none in the rule or in the shipped conventions page. A repo whose review is a mailing-list patch series therefore had nothing to bind any clause to, and the rule reads as not applying rather than as demanding anything. Fixed by binding the rule to the **reviewed change** and naming the shapes it can take (pull request as the paved road; a mailing-list patch series or a Gerrit/Phabricator change otherwise), with a new obligation rather than a relaxation: such a repo MUST name its unit of review in the branching decision. Nothing else in the rule moved - rebase onto the base, no back-merge, no change based on another open change, land by rebase-merge or squash-merge, the per-commit bar, the no-rewrite rule. The shipped conventions page, which carries the operational form of the same rule, gains one sentence saying the four bullets bind to that named unit. What is NOT claimed: no clone of torvalds/linux was assessed this round, and the change does not make that repo compliant - it merges subsystem trees rather than landing by rebase or squash, which stays a recorded deviation. What the case asked for is that the rule say something to a repo without pull requests, and it now does.

The other half of the same case, and it does not close with the vocabulary fix above. A merge queue that batches several changes and lands one two-parent commit is neither rebase-merge nor squash-merge, so the landing clause still refuses a shape that is in wide use. The tree's own record already anticipated it: ADR-026 lists a merge queue as the mitigation where signatures or exactly-tested commits matter, and its `Revisit when` section reserves the call - 'a context arrives where what ships must be the exact commit CI tested - then a merge queue, or merge commits read with --first-parent, wins on that repo's own record'. Adding a third compliant landing method to the rule would decide, inside a pull request, exactly what that record reserved for a record of its own, and it would also loosen the linear-history claim that ADR-026 is named after. Left open rather than guessed at.
observations.waiver: Owner decision, not unbuilt work. Two options, and they differ in what they cost. (a) Treat the queue's batch commit as an integration artifact rather than a unit of work: the rule keeps its bar per reviewed change, the batch commit is bookkeeping, and the mainline stops being linear - which contradicts the title and the branch-protection advice of the record that settled this. (b) Keep the two landing methods and require a queue to land by rebase or squash where its platform allows that, with a two-parent batch commit recorded as a deviation - narrower, but it tells a repo running the queue's default configuration that it is non-compliant for a property nobody has argued costs anything. Either way it supersedes part of ADR-026, which is a record's job, not a rule edit's.

observations.evidence: Reproduced by the case's procedure - a read of the schema rule against a migrations library's shape. The rule's antecedent was `A repo that owns a database MUST carry that schema as executable DDL under database/schema/`, and nothing after it addressed a repo that owns no database. For a library whose product is multi-backend migrations the antecedent is simply false, so the rule was silent about the artefact that repo actually ships - the DDL it emits into somebody else's database - while appearing to have covered the subject. Fixed by naming the second shape in the rule: a repo whose product is the schema change owns no database, so the schema directory and the typed twin do not apply and the repo says so once (which is the checklist rule's 'does not apply, said once', not an exemption); what it does own is the emitted DDL, per backend it claims to support, and that MUST be specified verbatim as an interface contract, differences between backends included. That is a new obligation on this shape, not a hole: before the change such a repo had no stated duty at all. What is NOT claimed: no oban-bg/oban checkout was cloned or assessed this round - the procedure this case defines is a read of the rule against that repo's known shape, and that is what was executed.

Reproduced by the case's first procedure step: `grep -rni -e jcheck -e gitreview` across the checkout returned hits only in docs/validation (the suite's own data and the generated pages) - zero in the intake step, zero in the eight assessment passes, zero in the adoption checkmap. Fixed in the three places that ask the questions those files answer. The intake step of the align skill gains a bullet next to the lifecycle-signal one, naming `.jcheck/conf` (reviewer role, reviewer count, issue tracker, commit-message form), `.gitreview` (the review host and project, which answers 'where does review happen' with 'not on the git host you are reading'), `CODEOWNERS` and `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/config.yml`, and instructing that they be opened before the question round and played back as confirmations - the same treatment the tracker inference already gets two bullets below. Assessment pass 2 detects them as decisions already written as data rather than as gaps. The adoption checkmap's Gate 0 brownfield cell names them in the same breath as the README/CONTRIBUTING lifecycle signal. What is NOT claimed: the procedure's second half - watching a real assessment of openjdk/jdk or qt/qtbase open the file - was not executed this round, so what is verified is that the instruction now exists where the questions are asked, not that an agent obeys it.

Reproduced by reading the skill, as the procedure says: spec-reconcile's step 2 detection list had four entries, none of them about code kept alive for an already-shipped contract, and step 3 read in full 'Resolve each: update the spec, fix the code, or explicitly record why. Prefer making the spec accurate to the real behavior.' Followed literally against a compatibility shim - a function body with no header, existing because a previous release's binary is the contract - that preference documents the shim as current design, which is the record getting worse rather than better. Fixed in both steps: detection now names the shape (a compatibility shim, a deprecated alias, a body with no header, a route kept alive for an old client), and resolution gives it a path of its own - its own subsection naming what it preserves and the condition for removing it, with the capability's contracts left describing the current shape. Deleting it from the spec is named as the opposite error, because it ships. What counts as a breaking change is explicitly left to the repo's own recorded decision rather than settled by this step. The engine's own capability spec carries the same requirement and an acceptance criterion, so the coupling guard has something to hold it to. What is NOT claimed: no qtbase checkout was assessed this round; the procedure is a read of the skill, and the shim shape it is read against comes from the earlier round's evidence.

Reproduced with the case's own command: `grep -rni fuzz` across the whole checkout, excluding docs/validation, returned 0 hits before the change. The axis catalog covered secrets, authn, authz, input validation, output/injection, transport, rate limiting, logging, dependencies, CI permissions, agent boundaries, data at rest, threat model and negative scope - every one of them a control or a policy, none of them the thing that actually finds the bugs in a repo that parses untrusted bytes. Fixed by an adversarial-testing axis: what actively tries to break this rather than confirm it works (fuzzing, property-based tests, a kept crash corpus, a red-team pass), where it runs, who triages a finding, and whether a crash becomes a regression test. The page's 'you have this case' section gains the matching block, citing FFmpeg as the case recorded in this suite's own targets file - six in-tree fuzz targets and no SECURITY.md. The same grep now returns 4 hits, all in docs/method/security-baseline.md. The axis binds like every other: 'not applicable' is an answer, silence is not, so the rule requiring a decision per axis now reaches this one.

Two halves, both re-run first, and only one of them is a pull request's to close. The runtime-cost half reproduced: the tooling rule said 'a Node runtime MUST be present to run them regardless of the repo's own language or stack' and named nothing else, while the shipped guards it points at are shell scripts - standard/.claude/hooks/lib.sh line 24 denies every command outright when jq is absent, and all three PreToolUse hooks in the settings baseline are .sh files invoked as commands. So the rule understated its own cost in exactly the direction that hurts most. Fixed: the rule now names a Node runtime, a POSIX shell and jq, says a repo that cannot supply them records the guards it consequently does not run as a deviation, and the prerequisites page gains a platform section - the guards are silent without a POSIX shell because a guard only prints when it denies, Git Bash or WSL supplies the shell with jq installed on top, and verifyAgentGuards.sh is the only positive evidence available. The settings-baseline half is NOT closed. Re-read this round: of the deny and ask lists in standard/.claude/settings.json, every destructive entry names a POSIX tool - sudo, su, rm -rf, dd, mkfs, diskutil, shred, shutdown, reboot, halt, killall, chmod, launchctl, crontab - so the same action spelled in another shell's vocabulary matches nothing and is neither denied nor queried. The page now states that boundary and tells the adopter to extend the lists and record what they added under the agent-boundaries axis, which is the honest half; shipping a second vocabulary is not.
observations.waiver: Owner decision on the remaining half. Writing deny patterns for a shell nobody here runs would produce entries that have never once fired on the platform they claim to cover - the same silence this whole batch is about, in a longer file - so the options are (a) ship a Windows/PowerShell vocabulary and stand behind it, which needs a machine to exercise it on and a maintainer willing to own the false sense of coverage until then, or (b) keep the baseline POSIX-only, as now, and treat the extension as the adopter's recorded deviation. Left failing rather than counted closed, because a team on that platform still gets no shipped protection from the settings baseline either way.

observations.evidence: Reproduced by the case's procedure, widened to the catalogue the title actually names: `grep -rni -e bazel -e cmake -e 'build graph' -e dialect -e sqlite` across the checkout, excluding docs/validation, returned one hit, in an unrelated paragraph of the align skill about stack archetypes. Neither the decision checklist nor the capability-map guidance had a category for a repo carrying two independently-authored descriptions of one structure - a Bazel BUILD graph beside a CMakeLists.txt, or one schema hand-forked into a second SQL dialect - and neither the coupling guard (code against its spec) nor schema-pair (DDL against its typed twin) sees that pair, because both sides are the same kind of artefact. Fixed by a checklist row: why it matters (neither copy is the source, so they drift and the drift surfaces on whichever platform nobody builds daily), the paved road (generate one from the other; where nothing can generate it, declare the pair and put a check behind the declaration), and the answer that is not available (two hand-edited copies with no declared edge). The row is honest about what ships: the standard already has a guard for the DDL/typed-twin pair and a declared-restatement mechanism for facts, and a build graph needs the repo's own equivalent - so this is a decision the repo must take, not a guard it inherits.

Reproduced by reading the two surfaces the case names. The buildable tier's required sections are Data contracts ('Tables / columns / types / constraints, enums, persisted JSONB or message/record shapes') and Interface contracts ('Every endpoint or public function... method + path... the request shape... the success response'), and the depth bar in the shipped specs README describes buildable as 'exact schemas and enums, every endpoint with its inputs, outputs and errors'. A repo whose product is narrative text, a translation catalogue or a packaging recipe has none of those, and the only reading available was the behavioral escape hatch - which is precisely wrong there, because such a repo does have contracts and often states them more exactly in its own artefacts than prose could. `grep -rni -e narrative -e translation -e 'packaging recipe' -e content-only` outside docs/validation returned nothing relevant to specs. Fixed on the template side, which is what the case's `then` asks for: the data contract is the artefact's own structure (a recipe's required variables, a catalogue's message ids and plural forms, a document's normative-statement conventions and anchors), the interface contract is what consumes the artefact and how that consumption fails, an artefact that already states a contract exactly is quoted verbatim and pointed at rather than paraphrased, and `behavioral` is named as NOT the alternate path. The depth bar in the specs README carries the pointer so the tier call is made with it in view. What is NOT closed: the third sub-finding recorded alongside this case on 2026-08-04 - a repo whose normative artefact is the document itself, where the coupling guard has an odd relationship with what counts as code - is outside this case's `then` and no case currently states it.

The only mechanical defect in the batch, and reproducing it changed what the fix had to be. Built a TTF-shaped fixture carrying 'Version 2.103' in a name table and declared it as a home, the way a font repo's canonical version fact would be. With the string as UTF-16, facts-check reported `FAIL font-version: the home pattern matches nothing in fonts/Demo-Regular.ttf` - which reads as a bad regular expression and sends the author to fix a pattern that was never the problem. With the identical string as an ASCII name record, the same declaration reported `ok font-version = 2.103 - 1 restatement(s) agree`: a green tick over a file the check cannot parse, and coverage claimed for a fact whose home it never really read. So the boundary was not merely unstated - the answer depended on which encoding the artefact happened to use. Fixed by routing all four home mechanisms and the claims path through one reader that refuses a file with a NUL byte in its first 8000 bytes, naming the boundary and the way out (a text home the artefact is built from, or an undeclared restatement stated as undeclared where it is restated). The script's header and the shipped file's own doc page state it in prose as well. Proved rather than asserted: tools/facts-check-test.mjs gains four cases and, with the refusal short-circuited, exactly three of them fail - the ASCII false pass, the UTF-16 misleading message, and a claim pointing into a binary - while the fourth, a text home in a repo that also ships binary artefacts, passes either way, which is the direction that had to stay intact. What is NOT claimed: no google/fonts checkout was assessed, and the check still cannot read a binary fact - the case asked for a stated boundary, not for a mechanism to cross it. The security-axis observation recorded alongside this case on 2026-08-04, about artefacts a repo publishes rather than executes, is outside this case's `then` and is not addressed.
